transcript:
Meeting header:
Date: 2025-08-29
Start: 15:30 PDT
Duration: ~58 minutes
Attendees: Alex Chen (Redwood AE), Priya Raman (Redwood SE), Samir Patel (NovaLogic CTO), Maria Gomez (Lead ML Eng), Tom Lee (SRE)

Auto-summary (auto-generated, may be rough):
- Deep dive into KV cache eviction/paging behavior observed during NovaLogic's long-chat workloads.
- Discussed prefix reuse causing collisions, prefetch ideas, TTL drift, and spill-to-disk paging.
- Agreed on telemetry exports, synthetic testing, and a Dedicated pilot to reproduce tail latency.

Topics: KV eviction, paging, prefix reuse/collisions, long-context memory pressure, batching tradeoffs, quantization impacts, VPC/on-prem constraints.

--- Transcript (timestamps approximate, transcription contains minor errors) ---
[00:00] Alex: Hey everyone, thanks for joining, we wanted to walk through the kv paging, and uh prefix collisions you folks flagged in your ticket. I have Priya from SE with me.
[00:10] Priya: Hi all. I skimmed the logs you sent and there are a couple of things that stand out. Before we jump in Samir, could you give a quick recap of what you see in prod?
[00:20] Samir: Yeah, sure. So in production we're getting periodic spikes in tail latency during our 20k concurrent user window. It's mostly when users open long conversations, like >8k tokens, and it looks like the token generation stalls for a couple hundred milliseconds intermittently. We also saw an uptick in 503s when the traffic bursts.
[00:40] Maria: To add, the hit rate on our app-level cache looked fine, but when we correlate with your telemetry, prefix hit rate drops sharply and eviction_rate shows bursts. I'm not sure if prefixes are being evicted because they're large or because of prefix id collision.
[00:55] Priya: Right. Two high-probability culprits: one is KV cache pressure from long-context sessions — the KV per-session footprint grows with longer conversation windows — and second is prefix reuse mapping collisions where multiple logical prefixes map to the same internal cache slot due to our sharding heuristics.
[01:10] Tom: Sorry, can you explain the prefix collision bit again? We thought each prefix was keyed by a hash. How do they collide at runtime?
[01:20] Priya: Yeah, good question. We use a hashed namespace across shards for the in-memory store. Collisions are rare on single items but when you have a hot prefix pattern — think many conversations reusing the same few initial messages — those prefixes become hotkeys and can cause eviction churn in adjacent buckets. The runtime also uses an approximate LRU that's bucketed, so a heavy write to a bucket can evict other prefixes pinned in that bucket.
[01:40] Alex: Also note that when we hit memory thresholds we fall back to a spill-to-disk paging path. That path is higher latency and can cause the observed 200-500ms stalls for certain token ranges.
[01:50] Maria: We do see spikes in 'kv_spillback' metrics aligning with user peak times. The spike is... it grows like a sawtooth.
[02:00] Priya: Right, and a sawtooth pattern is indicative of periodic full cache scans or batch eviction windows. Do you have per-prefix sizes available?
[02:08] Tom: We only have aggregate averages in the dashboard we shared. I can dig a bit deeper.
[02:12] Priya: Please. The distribution is what matters — a few very large prefixes can dominate memory.
[02:18] Samir: We do have several multi-turn assistant prototypes that keep a long-kv history per conversation for context. They reuse a common system prompt which is the same prefix across chats — so that could be the hot prefix you mean.
[02:34] Priya: Exactly. System prompt reuse + long per-session KV leads to two things: hot prefixes and ballooning per-session caches. The runtime's default policy favors global LRU with TTL, but the TTL and per-prefix eviction weight aren't tuned for these patterns.
[02:47] Alex: Quick note: we recently introduced a per-prefix weight setting and a prefetch hint API in the 2025-06 runtime. Those can be used to pin or change eviction priority for specific prefixes. Have you tried hints?
[02:59] Maria: Not yet, we didn't know that API existed in Hosted. We're on a slightly older hosted runtime version.
[03:05] Priya: Okay that explains part of it. If you update to the runtime with hint support, you can mark the system prompt prefixes as low-eviction (pin-lite) so they don't get evicted as aggressively. We also recommend prefix sharding alignment — avoid hashing short ids that collide into same buckets.
[03:20] Tom: You mentioned spill-to-disk. Can you describe the paging strategy? Is it synchronous? As in, every time the model needs keys it will block waiting for disk?
[03:30] Priya: The spill is async but there's a small synchronous read in the hot path for miss penalties. In the current implementation if a KV key is not in RAM and the request needs that key, the runtime issues an async fetch and then continues; but because the KV cache is used for KV cache decoding (e.g., past-key-values), the decoder waits for the key and that creates the tail latency. For long sequences there are many dependent cache lookups so the penalty multiplies.
[03:54] Samir: That matches what we see — long context sessions show multiplicative latency instead of additive.
[03:59] Priya: Multiplicative because of sequential dependency. One missed refill can stall many subsequent attention steps.
[04:05] Alex: There's also an interaction with batching. When you increase batch size to improve throughput, you increase the chance that batched requests touch different prefixes in the same bucket, increasing evictions. So throughput gains can harm tail latency unless you do intelligent request routing.
[04:22] Maria: Hmm we had bumped batch size to 64 to reduce token cost but saw worse tail latency during the peak. So that checks out.
[04:30] Priya: For your workload we typically recommend adaptive batching plus prefix-aware batching. That means when a request arrives, the router attempts to co-locate requests with similar prefix hashes so they share cached keys. Also enable per-route cache affinity if you have tenant-scoped models.
[04:44] Tom: Is that a config we can set in Hosted or requires Dedicated?
[04:48] Alex: Affinity and pinning are available on Hosted in the newer runtime tiers but finer-grained bucket adjustments and custom sharding are Dedicated-only. Given your size, Dedicated pilot would let us repro with your exact sharding and memory limits.
[05:00] Maria: Security-wise, Dedicated also fits our VPC/KMS constraints better.
[05:04] Samir: We also have on-prem roadmaps for regulated clients. If we test on Dedicated and it reduces eviction, would that translate to on-prem?
[05:12] Priya: The runtime behavior is the same across modes. Differences are in networking and KMS integrations. On-prem will give you full control over memory allocation, and you can attach an NVMe-backed spill with tuned async prefetchers to reduce read latency.
[05:27] Tom: Speaking of prefetch, do you have heuristics for what to prefetch? We tried naive prefetching a week ago and it caused even more eviction churn.
[05:36] Priya: Prefetching must be selective. Two strategies: LRU-proximity prefetch for immediate neighbors, and ML-based predictive prefetch using recent prefix access sequences. Naive blanket prefetching inflates memory usage and triggers eviction. You should prefetch only when the predicted hit probability > threshold (e.g., >0.6) and size is small relative to free memory.
[05:56] Maria: Do you guys expose predictive prefetch models or example configs?
[06:00] Priya: We can share a config and a sample predictive model that uses an n-gram of prefix ids. It runs cheap and integrates into the router. We'll include that in the telemetry export.
[06:10] Samir: We saw something labeled 'kv_ttl_drift' in one of the metrics. What is that?
[06:15] Priya: TTL drift is when background eviction runs or autoscaler rebalances result in a TTL counter divergence — keys that should have expired earlier stick around because their bucket wasn't scanned, or conversely get evicted prematurely. It often shows up when you have dynamic scaling events.
[06:29] Alex: Yes, especially during scale-up/scale-down churn. If new nodes join, the hash ring changes and keys can be temporarily orphaned or double-counted leading to transient evictions.
[06:38] Tom: We did have a couple of autoscaler events in the window that correlates.
[06:42] Priya: If that's frequent you can enable sticky routing for sessions so they stick to a node with their cached keys; it reduces cross-node misses during autoscale. It's a tradeoff with load balancing though.
[06:54] Maria: On quantization — one of our infra folks suggested dropping to 4-bit to halve KV memory. Does that sound feasible?
[07:02] Priya: Quantization of model weights reduces model memory, but KV storage is usually activations/past-key-values which are not always safe to aggressively quantize. We've done experiments with 8-bit quantized KV where the performance loss is minimal, but 4-bit introduces numeric instability for long-context attention and can actually increase decoding errors. For KV-heavy workloads, 8-bit or mixed-precision with lossy compression is safer.
[07:28] Alex: Another option is to compress older prefixes with a more aggressive lossy codec and keep recent prefixes in higher fidelity. That way you reduce memory without touching live decoding precision.
[07:38] Samir: Interesting. Could Redwood support a tiered-KV where cold prefixes are compressed and hot prefixes are full fidelity?
[07:45] Priya: Yes, that's what we call cold-tier spill + on-demand decompression. On Dedicated/on-prem you can tune the thresholds and the codec. On Hosted we have preset profiles: moderate, aggressive, and none. We'll share recommended profiles for long-context chat apps.
[07:59] Tom: For the spill storage you mentioned NVMe — do you have recommendations around IO depth, async queue sizes?
[08:05] Priya: For NVMe spill use a shallow async queue (depth 32-64) and larger readahead for sequential scans. Avoid synchronous syncfs calls; rely on direct-io and our async prefetch pipeline. We'll include recommended kernel/tuning knobs in the security doc we send.
[08:22] Maria: Ok, action items and then I'll get the team to run the synthetic test. Can you outline the minimal telemetry you need to reproduce?
[08:30] Priya: Sure. Minimum: per-prefix hit/miss counts, per-prefix size histogram, eviction events with reason (age/weight/pressure), spill read latency by key, node-level free-memory, autoscaler events with timestamps, and router-batch composition (which prefixes were batched together). Please include a 30-min contiguous window around an incident.
[08:53] Tom: We can pull that; expect one export for Aug 27 09:00 UTC incident.
[08:58] Alex: Great. We'll also attach a short checklist for runtime flags: pin hints, prefix-affinity, adaptive-batching, and prefetch thresholds.
[09:06] Samir: If we push pin hints, will that increase cost because of extra memory? We are cost sensitive.
[09:12] Alex: It will increase memory usage for pinned items but it often reduces overall cost by preventing repeated expensive disk reads and retransmissions. Net effect should be neutral-to-positive for unit economics. Redwood Optimize can estimate the delta if you give us token distribution.
[09:25] Maria: We'll share token distribution with you in the same telemetry export.
[09:29] Priya: One more gotcha — prefix canonicalization. If your app hashes slightly different representations (trailing whitespace, punctuation) you'll create many logically-equal prefixes. Dedup before hashing.
[09:41] Maria: Oh, we do have some inconsistent trimming code in one microservice. Good catch.
[09:45] Tom: Question: what about eviction notification hooks? We'd like to log when a pinned prefix gets evicted unexpectedly.
[09:52] Priya: There is a webhook/trace event that can emit eviction reasons to your logging sink. We can enable verbose eviction tracing for the pilot window. It has a slight overhead but invaluable for debugging.
[10:03] Samir: Sounds good.
[10:05] Alex: Ok let's recap next steps quickly. Priya will drop the telemetry export format and an example prefetch config. Alex will send Dedicated pilot terms. NovaLogic will run synthetic burst test and export logs. We'll re-convene after the telemetry review.
[10:20] Maria: Thanks all. One last thing — any quick mitigation we can do that morning if we see another incident?
[10:26] Priya: Short-term: reduce batch size, temporarily increase cache capacity (if on Hosted you can request a scale-up burst), enable pin hints for the system prompt, and reduce prefetch aggressiveness. That should reduce tail.
[10:38] Tom: We'll prepare a runbook with those steps.
[10:42] Alex: Great, we should be able to follow up with a 1-hour triage session once you share the telemetry. Thanks everybody.
[10:50] Samir: Appreciate it.
[10:52] End call.
